params.question: During childhood, GnRH secretion is minimal despite the hypothalamic-pituitary axis being anatomically intact. What is the most accurate explanation for this quiescence?

answers.text: The pituitary gonadotrophs are not yet mature enough to respond to GnRH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pituitary gonadotrophs are structurally mature in childhood; they simply do not receive sufficient GnRH stimulation because the upstream KNDy neurons are suppressed.

answers.text: Ovarian follicles are absent until puberty begins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primordial follicles are present in the ovary from birth. It is the lack of FSH drive, not follicle absence, that keeps them quiescent.

answers.text: KNDy neurons in the arcuate nucleus are actively suppressed, preventing GnRH pulsatility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. KNDy neurons act as the GnRH pulse generator; their active suppression during childhood keeps GnRH, LH, and FSH levels very low until the brake is released at puberty.

answers.text: High levels of circulating oestradiol maintain negative feedback throughout childhood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oestradiol levels are actually very low in prepubertal girls. The quiescence is not due to negative feedback but to active suppression of the GnRH pulse generator itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key point is that the HPO axis is structurally intact in childhood but functionally suppressed. KNDy neurons in the arcuate nucleus are held in check; once that suppression lifts at puberty, GnRH pulses begin and the entire axis activates.

Exactly right. The KNDy neurons in the arcuate nucleus function as a pulse generator for GnRH. Their active suppression during childhood is the primary reason the HPO axis remains quiescent until puberty.

interactions.label: A 16-year-old girl presents with absent breast development and primary amenorrho

params.question: A 16-year-old girl presents with absent breast development and primary amenorrhoea. Her serum FSH is markedly elevated. Which level of the reproductive axis is most likely dysfunctional?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hypothalamic failure would result in low FSH due to insufficient GnRH stimulation, not elevated FSH.
Pituitary failure would cause low, not high, FSH. The elevated FSH here indicates the pituitary is responding appropriately to low oestradiol levels.

answers.text: Gonads — ovarian failure with loss of negative feedback

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Non-functioning ovaries produce insufficient oestradiol, removing negative feedback on the pituitary. The pituitary compensates by increasing FSH output, resulting in hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.
Outflow obstruction causes amenorrhoea but does not affect gonadotrophin levels. Breast development would be present since ovarian function is intact, and FSH would be normal.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the gonadotrophin logic: elevated FSH and LH means the pituitary is trying harder because it is receiving insufficient negative feedback from the ovaries. This pattern — hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism — points to gonadal failure, not a central cause.
Well analysed. Elevated gonadotrophins with absent secondary sexual characteristics is the hallmark of gonadal failure — the pituitary is responding appropriately to the lack of ovarian oestradiol.

interactions.label: A 14-year-old girl with Turner syndrome is brought for management of delayed pub

params.question: A 14-year-old girl with Turner syndrome is brought for management of delayed puberty. Which approach is most appropriate for initiating pubertal development?

answers.text: Reassurance and watchful waiting, since puberty will occur spontaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This approach suits constitutional delay, not Turner syndrome. In Turner syndrome (45,X), the streak gonads cannot produce oestrogen, so spontaneous puberty will not occur.

answers.text: Immediate high-dose combined oral contraceptive pill to accelerate development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: High-dose oestrogen given too quickly can compromise final adult height by accelerating epiphyseal fusion. Oestrogen must be introduced gradually, starting with low doses.

answers.text: Gradual oestrogen replacement timed to bone age, alongside growth hormone therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Turner syndrome requires carefully titrated oestrogen starting around age 12–13, matched to bone age to protect final height, combined with growth hormone, cardiac surveillance, and thyroid monitoring as part of multidisciplinary care.

answers.text: Pulsatile GnRH therapy to stimulate her own ovarian function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulsatile GnRH works when the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is intact but unstimulated, as in Kallmann syndrome. In Turner syndrome the gonads themselves are dysgenetic and cannot respond even if gonadotrophins are adequate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Turner syndrome involves gonadal failure from streak gonads, so exogenous oestrogen replacement is essential — spontaneous puberty will not occur. The key is starting gradually around age 12–13, timed to bone age, combined with growth hormone to optimise final height.
Correct. Turner syndrome demands gradual oestrogen replacement timed to bone age alongside growth hormone, with lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up including cardiac and thyroid surveillance.

interactions.label: A 6-year-old girl is diagnosed with central precocious puberty and started on a

params.question: A 6-year-old girl is diagnosed with central precocious puberty and started on a GnRH analogue. What is the mechanism by which this drug halts pubertal progression?

answers.text: It blocks oestrogen receptors in target tissues such as breast and uterus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oestrogen receptor blockers like tamoxifen work peripherally. GnRH analogues act centrally at the pituitary level, not at target tissues.

answers.text: It provides continuous GnRH, which downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Normal GnRH acts in pulses; the analogue delivers it continuously, which paradoxically desensitises and downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors, shutting down LH and FSH secretion.

answers.text: It inhibits adrenal androgen production at the zona reticularis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GnRH analogues act on the pituitary gonadotrophin axis, not on the adrenal glands. Adrenal androgen production is controlled by ACTH, not GnRH.

answers.text: It directly suppresses KNDy neuron firing in the arcuate nucleus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GnRH analogues act on the pituitary's GnRH receptors, not on the hypothalamic KNDy neurons. The effect is downstream of GnRH release, at the receptor level.

overallFeedback.feedback: GnRH analogues exploit a pharmacological paradox: while pulsatile GnRH stimulates gonadotrophin release, continuous delivery desensitises and downregulates the pituitary GnRH receptors, effectively switching the reproductive axis off.

Exactly right. The key pharmacological insight is that continuous GnRH delivery paradoxically suppresses the axis by downregulating pituitary GnRH receptors — the opposite of what the normal pulsatile pattern achieves.
